title: Convergence Analysis of Newton's Method for Neural Networks in the Overparameterized Limit
claim: Regularized second-order preconditioning lifts the vanishing kernel eigenvalue spectrum and lowers loss, with the effect growing as regularization shrinks.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, left-to-right, shared viridis color gradient legend
description: Two side-by-side line plots share a viridis-style color gradient that encodes the regularizer parameter gamma, from 1e-1 (dark purple) to 1e-10 (light green). Left panel (a): eigenvalue lambda_m on a log scale against eigenvalue index m from 1 to 16. A bold red curve for the standard NTK falls steeply from 1 to about 1e-14. Each NNTK curve with a smaller gamma sits higher and flatter, so the curves form a fan of parallel descending lines. Right panel (b): relative loss after one Newton step on log-log axes against network width N from 10 to 1e6. Each gamma has a line with markers and a shaded band for variation across runs, plus a dashed horizontal asymptote. Smaller gamma gives lower loss that keeps falling as width grows. Both panels have legends, and the caption below each panel is written as (a) and (b).
caption: Empirical validation of Remarks 5 and 6 for a shallow tanh NN (1) with β = 0.52 on M = 16 samples of y = 2x + 0.4 sin(5πx). (Results in (b) are averaged across 100 runs.)
abstract: A convergence analysis is developed for the regularized Newton method for training neural networks (NNs) in the overparameterized limit. As the number of hidden units tends to infinity, the NN training dynamics converge in probability to the solution of a deterministic limit equation involving a "Newton neural tangent kernel" (NNTK). Explicit rates characterizing this convergence are provided and, in the infinite-width limit, we prove that the NN converges exponentially fast to the target data (i.e., a global minimizer with zero loss). We show that this convergence is uniform across the frequency spectrum, addressing the spectral bias inherent in gradient descent. The eigenvalues of the NTK for gradient descent accumulate at zero, leading to slow convergence for target data with high-frequency components. In contrast, the NNTK has uniformly lower bounded eigenvalues if the regularization parameter is selected appropriately, allowing Newton's method to converge more quickly for data with high-frequency components. Mathematical challenges that need to be addressed include the implicit parameter update of the Newton method with a potentially indefinite Hessian matrix and the fact that the dimension of this linear system of equations tends to infinity as the NN width grows. This substantially complicates deriving the training dynamics in the overparameterized limit as well as proving the convergence of the finite-width dynamics thereto. Our analysis identifies a scaling formula for selecting the regularization parameter, which we show can vanish at a suitable rate as the NN width becomes larger. In addition, we prove that, for sufficiently large numbers of hidden units, the regularized Hessian remains positive definite during training and the Newton updates for individual NN parameters converge to zero, demonstrating that the model behaves as a linearization around the initialization.
